old: Two old words for 'making smaller' — one Germanic, one French — ended up fused into a single English verb.
It can mean chopping food into tiny pieces, but also softening your words so they land less harshly.
It shares a root with the Swedish word minska, 'to reduce,' and with the tiny English word min.
clues: This verb used in kitchens comes partly from an Old English word meaning 'to make less or smaller,' and partly from a French word for 'slender, slight.'
It means to cut food, especially meat, onions or garlic, into very tiny pieces, much finer than a rough chop or neat dice.
Someone blunt doesn't do this to their words, and it also describes walking with short, dainty, affected steps.
